sentences.text: 1. Vide this judgment, I shall dispose of the appeal against the order dated 03.06.2015 ("the impugned order" in short) passed by the Ld. Adjudicating Officer, (District) New Delhi ("ADM" in short), directing the appellant to pay a consolidated penalty of Rs.2.5 lacs for M/s Buttercup Confectionery Ltd & Ors.

Vs FSO Page No. 1 of 17 selling substandard food as well as misbranding of the same, in violation of Section 26(2)(ii) & Section 27(1) r/w Section 3(1)(i) of the Food Safety and Standards Act, 2006 ("FSS Act" in short) and Regulation no.2.2.2.5(ii)(b) of the Food Safety &
Standards (Packaging & Labelling) Regulations, 2011 ("FSS (P&L) Regulations" in short).
2. Facts in brief as per the appeal are that on 11.11.2012, Food Safety Officer ("FSO" in short), had taken the sample of "Chocolate", from the premises of M/s Buttercup Confectionery Ltd., Inderpuri,
New Delhi, for analysis.
The Food Analyst vide his report dated 26.11.2012 opined that the sample contains extraneous matter viz. added vegetable fats in contravention of Section 3(1) (i)of the FSS Act.
He further opined that the sample was also found misbranded because there was violation of Regulation No. 2.2.2.5(ii)(b) of FSS (P&L) Regulation, 2011.

The Food Safety Officer filed a complaint/application under Rule 3.1.1(3) FSS Rules, 2011 before the Ld. ADM alleging violation of Section 26(2)

Regulation, punishable under Sections 52 of FSS Act.

sentences.text: Notice of the same was issued to the appellant and hearing was given.

3. The appellant has challenged the impugned order inter alia on the grounds among others that Ld.
ADM failed to appreciate the evidence on record i.e. the Form VA wherein FSO not only wrongly M/s Buttercup Confectionery Ltd & Ors.
Vs FSO Page No. 2 of 17 described the sample of "Fundoo Chocolate" as "Chocolate" but also illegally applied the standards of Milk Chocolate, which is different article of food.

The "Fundoo Chocolate" is of the category of Filled Chocolates which contained confectionery in the centre distinct in composition from the outer covering Fundoo Chocolate, which was of Chocolate only.
Ld. ADM failed to appreciate that the sanction of the case is bad in law as the Designated Officer did not accord sanction of Milk Chocolate to institute the prosecution against the appellant.
The Food Analyst had no authority to change the nomenclature of food article.

The Ld. ADM wrongly relied upon the contention of the Food Analyst that central and outer portion of the Fundoo Chocolate were not distinct as the Food Analyst had brought the package of remnants of the sample during crossexamination after long lapse of time, which were stored at room temperature and because of this, the central portion and outer portion of the Fundoo Chocolate had got diminished.

It is well known that Chocolates cannot be properly stored at room temperature as it cannot retain its original shape at the room temperature and required to be stored at a temperature of 16 to 20 degree centigrade for proper storage.
The Ld. ADM did not appreciate that on the notice of Form VA, the FSO had noted down the declaration as "contains added flavor".
The only allegation against the company could be that label does not contain the name of flavor.
The declaration of labeling regulations was not required as the packages were not of the category of pre packed packages.

The Ld. ADM failed to appreciate that the word "Fundoo"
M/s Buttercup Confectionery Ltd & Ors.
Vs FSO Page No. 3 of 17 was not the brand name of the chocolate.
The brand name was given on the packages as "Choco Swiss" and the same was also noted down by the Food Analyst in his report.

The relevant para quoted in the said judgment of Nemi Chand (Supra), is reproduced as under :
"3.
It is not in dispute that the charge against the appellant was only of sub standardization of goods.

Mr. Sushil Kumar Jain, learned senior counsel appearing for the appellant, submits that though the appellant has some prima facie case even on merits, he would be giving up the plea on merits and his only submission is about the sentence which has been imposed by the courts below.

He has in this behalf,
argued that there has been an amendment in the Act by the Central Amendment Act 34 of 1976 whereby Section 16A was added and under the said section, only a fine is leviable.

He has drawn our attention to the judgment of this Court in 'T. Barai v.
Henry Ah Hoe and Another' [1982 (2) FAC 362] [1983 (1) SCC 177] wherein this Court held that since the amendment was beneficial to the accused persons, it can be applied even with respect to earlier cases as well which are pending in the Court.

entities.text:
T. Barai v.
Henry Ah Hoe and Another' [1982 (2) FAC 362] [1983 (1) SCC 177]
entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text:
In the said judgment, the Court held as under:
"22.
It is only retroactive criminal legislation that is prohibited under Article 20(1).

The prohibition contained in Article 20(1) is that no person shall be convicted of any offence except for violation of a law in force at the time of the commission of the act charged as an offence prohibits nor shall M/s Buttercup Confectionery Ltd & Ors.
Vs FSO Page No. 13 of 17 he be subjected to a penalty greater than that which might have been inflicted under the law in force at the time of the commission of the offence.

It is quite clear that insofar as the Central Amendment Act creates new offences or enhances punishment for a particular type of offence no person can be convicted by such ex post facto law nor can the enhanced punishment prescribed by the amendment be applicable.

But insofar as the Central Amendment Act reduces the punishment for an offence punishable under Section 16(1) (a) of the Act, there is no reason why the accused should not have the benefit of such reduced punishment.
The rule of beneficial construction requires that even ex post facto law of such a type should be applied to mitigate the rigour of the law.
The principle is based both on sound reason and common sense.
This finds support in the following passage from Crales on Statute Law, 7th Edn., at pp. 38889:
A retrospective statute is different from an ex post facto statute.
"Every ex post facto law...." said Chase, J., in the American case of Calder v. Bull "must necessarily be retrospective, but every retrospective law is not an ex post facto law.

Every law that takes away or impairs rights vested agreeably to existing laws is retrospective, and is generally unjust and may be oppressive; it is a good general rule that a law should have no retrospect, but in cases in which the laws may justly and for the benefit of the community and also of individuals relate to a time antecedent to their commencement: as statutes of oblivion or of pardon.

They are certainly retrospective,
and literally both concerning and after the facts committed.

But I do not consider any law ex post facto within the prohibition that mollifies the rigour of the criminal law,

7 but only those that create or aggravate the crime, or increase the punishment or change the rules of evidence for the purpose of conviction....

Old stock and printed material was already admitted before the Ld. ADM.
It was observed and found before the Ld. ADM during trial of the case that the package presented by the food analyst was the actual package and the same was ready for sale to individual customer.
The product was having extraneous material which was not permitted as per the provisions of the said Act and Regulations discussed above.
The case of the misbranding of the article collected from premises of the appellant has been proved before the Ld. ADM against the appellant.

However, considering the facts and circumstances of the case of misbranding of the product, the impugned order dt. 03.06.2015 is modified to the extent that the penalty of Rs.1,00,000/ is imposed for misbranding upon the appellant, meaning thereby, the appellant has to pay consolidated penalty of Rs.1,50,000/ (Rs.50,000/ for substandard and Rs.1,00,000/ for misbranding) instead of Rs.2,50,000/.
The consolidated penalty amount of Rs.1,50,000/ shall be deposited by the appellant within 30 days from the date of this order before the Ld. ADM.
Accordingly, this appeal is partly allowed.

opennyai_summary.facts:

Standards (Packaging & Labelling) Regulations, 2011 ("FSS (P&L) Regulations" in short).
2. Facts in brief as per the appeal are that on 11.11.2012, Food Safety Officer ("FSO" in short), had taken the sample of "Chocolate", from the premises of M/s Buttercup Confectionery Ltd., Inderpuri,
New Delhi, for analysis.
The Food Safety Officer filed a complaint/application under Rule 3.1.1(3) FSS Rules, 2011 before the Ld. ADM alleging violation of Section 26(2)

opennyai_summary.arguments:
The "Fundoo Chocolate" is of the category of Filled Chocolates which contained confectionery in the centre distinct in composition from the outer covering Fundoo Chocolate, which was of Chocolate only.
The Food Analyst had no authority to change the nomenclature of food article.
The Ld. ADM wrongly relied upon the contention of the Food Analyst that central and outer portion of the Fundoo Chocolate were not distinct as the Food Analyst had brought the package of remnants of the sample during crossexamination after long lapse of time, which were stored at room temperature and because of this, the central portion and outer portion of the Fundoo Chocolate had got diminished.
The declaration of labeling regulations was not required as the packages were not of the category of pre packed packages.
The sampled article Fundoo Chocolate was tested illegally as Milk Chocolate and the Food Analyst had no authority to consider and treat the Fundoo chocolate as milk chocolate.
The FSO is not authorized to change the nomenclature of the food article.
As per judgment in Municipal Corporation of Delhi vs Nand Kishore, it is only when the process of manufacture is complete then it can be said that an article of food has been manufactured for sale.
Danisco (India) Private Limited versus Union of India and another 2014 (2) FAC 109.
The sample was of a milk chocolate under regulation 2.7.4.1 of Food Safety and Standards (Food Product and Additive) Regulation, 2011.
The vegetable fats was diagnosed during the investigation.
In the present case, the appellant did not comply with the standards of Rules/Regulations of the Food Safety &
Standard Act.
The food analyst did not adopt the correct method of analysis in analyzing the central and outer covering portion separately which resulted in wrong opinion about the nature of food commodity.
The food analyst had no authority to change the nomenclature of food article.
opennyai_summary.issue: In this case, the only question to be determined is whether the article complies with the standards laid down or not?
opennyai_summary.ANALYSIS:
M/S Buttercup Confectionary Ltd vs Food Safety Officer on 30 October, 2019 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/69080198/
5 13.
The complaint/application under Rule 3.1.1 (3) of Food Safety and Standards Rules, 2011 was filed before the Ld. Adjudicating Officer / ADM, by the FSO for adjudication of the offence for violation of Section 26(2)(ii) & 27 of the FSS Act, 2006 r/w/s 3(1)(i) of the FSS Act, 2006 and Regulation no.2.2.2.5(ii)(b) of FSS (P&L) Regulations, which is punishable u/s 52 of FSS Act.
, found that the respondent therein appellant herein violated the provisions under Section 26 (2)(ii) & 27 of the FSS Act, 2006 r/w/s 3(1)(i) of the FSS Act, 2006 and Regulation no.2.2.2.5(ii)(b) of FSS (P&L)
Regulations, which is punishable u/s 52 of FSS Act, 2006 being of misbranded and substandard food.
It is quite clear that insofar as the Central Amendment Act creates new offences or enhances punishment for a particular type of offence no person can be convicted by such ex post facto law nor can the enhanced punishment prescribed by the amendment be applicable.
But insofar as the Central Amendment Act reduces the punishment for an offence punishable under Section 16(1) (a) of the Act, there is no reason why the accused should not have the benefit of such reduced punishment.
The rule of beneficial construction requires that even ex post facto law of such a type should be applied to mitigate the rigour of the law.
In the present case, there is nothing on record to show that the FSO insisted the appellant for selling of the food article.
The form VA was filled before sample was sealed with the cellotape.
The process of analyzing of the collected sample articles started immediately after receiving from the premises of the appellant.
The report was prepared by the Food Analyst and no appeal was preferred against the said report by the appellant.
The case of the misbranding of the article collected from premises of the appellant has been proved before the Ld. ADM against the appellant.
opennyai_summary.decision:
However, considering the facts and circumstances of the case of misbranding of the product, the impugned order dt. 03.06.2015 is modified to the extent that the penalty of Rs.1,00,000/ is imposed for misbranding upon the appellant, meaning thereby, the appellant has to pay consolidated penalty of Rs.1,50,000/ (Rs.50,000/ for substandard and Rs.1,00,000/ for misbranding) instead of Rs.2,50,000/.
The consolidated penalty amount of Rs.1,50,000/ shall be deposited by the appellant within 30 days from the date of this order before the Ld. ADM.
Accordingly, this appeal is partly allowed.
TCR be sent back along with copy of this judgment.
Appeal file be consigned to record room.
